opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's absolutely central. One of the things I've long been interested in is the idea that our capacity for abstract thought is grounded in, and grows out of, our everyday physical interactions with the world. As children, we learn how objects behave: things fall when you drop them, containers hold things, you can push something along a path, things can be in front of or behind other things. These are the sort of embodied, common-sense concepts that we acquire simply by being creatures with bodies moving around in a world of objects.

What's really interesting is how these concepts then get repurposed for much more abstract domains. Lakoff and Johnson made this point very powerfully with their work on conceptual metaphor. We talk about ideas being "in" our minds, as if the mind were a container. We talk about arguments having "foundations," or a line of reasoning "going somewhere." We speak of time as if it were space: the future is "ahead" of us, the past "behind." Even mathematics, arguably the most abstract thing we do, seems to borrow heavily from these primitive spatial and physical intuitions. Think of sets as containers, or numbers as points along a line.

So my view is that these embodied concepts aren't just a quaint developmental stage we pass through. They're more like scaffolding that remains in place, and abstract thought is in a sense built on top of it, by analogy and metaphor. That's partly why I've been interested in whether artificial systems need something similar. If you want an AI with genuinely general intelligence, with the kind of robust common sense that lets it extrapolate sensibly to novel situations, it might need a comparable foundation, whether that comes from actual embodiment, say in robotics, or from rich simulated 3D environments where agents can learn the basic physics of everyday objects.

Now, large language models complicate the picture in a fascinating way, because they've picked up an enormous amount of this structure second-hand, through text written by embodied humans. They can talk fluently about containers and paths and forces. Whether that amounts to the same kind of grounded understanding is a very open and interesting question. My hunch is that there's something missing, that the concepts are there in a sort of shadow form, inherited from us, but not anchored in the way ours are. But I hold that view with a degree of humility, because these systems keep surprising us.

r001.rationale: It says children acquire common-sense concepts by interacting physically with objects in the world.

r002.rationale: It states that abstract thought is built on embodied concepts, repurposed through analogy and metaphor.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is one of the really deep questions about cognition, actually, and it goes back a long way for me. When I started out in AI, I was very much in the classical symbolic tradition, working on logic-based approaches to common sense reasoning, and the thing you keep bumping into there is that so much of our everyday understanding of the world is bound up with the fact that we have bodies. We know what it is for something to be heavy, or for a container to hold liquid, or for an object to be out of reach, not because we've learned a set of axioms about those things but because we've lived them. We've pushed things, dropped things, spilled things.

And the interesting claim, which you find in people like Lakoff and Johnson, and in the broader embodied cognition literature, is that this doesn't just stay at the level of the concrete. It bleeds into our most abstract thinking. When we talk about "grasping" an idea, or an argument "falling apart," or someone being "under" pressure, those are not just decorative figures of speech. There's a reasonable case that the conceptual scaffolding we use for abstract domains, mathematics, ethics, even logic, is built on top of, or at least borrows its structure from, these very basic sensorimotor schemas: containment, support, path and goal, force and resistance.

Now, I want to be a bit careful here, because I don't think the strong version of that thesis is obviously right. I'm not convinced that every abstract concept is reducible to some embodied metaphor. But I do think the weaker version is very hard to deny, which is that our abstract thought is pervasively shaped by the fact that we are creatures who move around in a spatial world, who manipulate objects, who have to deal with other agents who also have bodies. Even something like the notion of an object, a thing that persists through time and can be in one place and not another, is a fairly sophisticated achievement, and it's rooted in that embodied engagement.

Where this becomes really pressing, of course, is with large language models. Here you have systems that have an enormous amount of knowledge about the world, in some sense, that can talk fluently about heavy objects and spilled liquids and ideas falling apart, but have never had a body, never pushed anything. So the question is whether what they have acquired from text is a kind of shadow or echo of embodied understanding, enough to be useful, enough to be impressive, but missing something fundamental. And I genuinely think that's an open question. There's a Wittgensteinian point lurking here too, that the meanings of our words are bound up with the forms of life in which they're used, and a form of life is an embodied, social thing. So I'm a bit wary of saying these models "understand" in the full sense, while at the same time being quite astonished at how far you can get without the body at all.

r001.rationale: The response says everyday understanding is bound up with having bodies and comes from lived experience, including pushing, dropping, and spilling things.

r002.rationale: It states that abstract thinking borrows from basic sensorimotor schemas such as containment, support, path and goal, and force and resistance.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think a great deal of our abstract thought is grounded in the concepts we acquire through being embodied creatures acting in a world. We encounter objects, move around them, put things inside other things, and learn that our actions have consequences. Those give us a repertoire of concepts that we can then use far beyond their original setting.

Take the idea of a path. You start somewhere, you have a destination, and you may encounter obstacles along the way. That structure carries over very naturally into thinking about a mathematical proof or a political project. We talk about making progress, getting stuck, or finding a way around a difficulty. These aren't merely decorative expressions; they can help organise the thought itself.

But I would distinguish that claim from the stronger claim that every system capable of abstract thought must have a body like ours. Understanding how human concepts arise is one question; understanding what other mechanisms could support comparable abilities is another. The interesting challenge is explaining how those very concrete, practical foundations become resources for the extraordinary flexibility of human thinking.

r001.rationale: The response says abstract thought is grounded in concepts acquired through being embodied and acting in the world, with examples of encountering objects and moving around them.

r002.rationale: It explains that physical concepts such as paths, destinations, and obstacles carry over to abstract domains like mathematical proofs and political projects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think embodied common sense provides a kind of foundation for abstract thought. We learn about objects, space, movement, containment, and agency through interacting with the world, and we then draw on those concepts when we reason about things that have no obvious physical form. We talk about being “in” trouble, “moving towards” a solution, or one idea “supporting” another. Those expressions suggest that some of the structure of our abstract thinking comes from our understanding of the physical world.

But I would distinguish that claim from the stronger claim that every instance of abstract thought requires a bodily simulation. Language allows us to build on concepts, combine them, and acquire concepts through other people. So you can get quite a long way from the original sensorimotor grounding. The interesting question is how much of that grounding has to be present in an individual thinker, and how much can be inherited through language and culture.

r001.rationale: The response says people learn concepts such as objects, space, movement, and agency through interacting with the world.

r002.rationale: It says people draw on those physically grounded concepts to reason about abstract topics, with examples such as being “in” trouble and moving toward a solution.
